label: START F3
title: Proton pump inhibitor with an NSAID
statement: Proton pump inhibitor with short-term (< 2 weeks) or longer-term (> 2 weeks) NSAID.

source.document: O'Mahony D, et al. STOPP/START criteria for potentially inappropriate prescribing in older people: version 3. Eur Geriatr Med 2023;14:625-632, Appendix 1 (corrected supplementary file; NHS Somerset copy used for text, sentence-identical to the earlier parse)

plain_summary: An anti-inflammatory pain medicine (NSAID) can damage the stomach lining, so a proton pump inhibitor should be taken with it, even for a short course.

medicine_groups.name: Proton pump inhibitors (medicines that meet this criterion)
medicine_groups.note: Tablets, capsules and granules count. Nexium Hp7 is esomeprazole with two antibiotics. Vimovo is naproxen with esomeprazole. Acimax contains omeprazole as omeprazole magnesium. Generic packs that show the ingredient name with a company name count too.

medicine_groups.name: NSAIDs, the anti-inflammatory pain medicines (the medicines whose supply raises the check)

ibuprofen: Advil Childrens Pain and Fever 2 to 7 Years
Advil Childrens Pain and Fever 7 to 12 Years
Advil Childrens Pain and Fever Relief 2 to 12 Years
Advil Infants Pain and Fever Relief 3 Months to 2 Years
Nurofen for Children 3 Months to 5 Years

medicine_groups.note: Systemic tablets, capsules, liquids and suppositories count. Systemic ketorolac injection, including Toradol, also counts. Exclude local treatments such as skin gels, creams, topical patches, plasters, sprays, eye drops and throat lozenges. Aspirin is not in this group. Vimovo already contains a proton pump inhibitor. Arthrotec contains misoprostol, which protects the stomach but is not a proton pump inhibitor. Generic packs that show the ingredient name with a company name count too.

rule_for_models: Apply this check only to a person aged 65 or over. If age is unknown, establish eligibility before reporting an omission. Make no finding when the record documents a contraindication to the proposed treatment, another valid clinical reason for omitting it, or end-of-life care with a palliative focus. Check each systemic Group B NSAID course, short or long, for cover by a Group A proton pump inhibitor. Look for overlapping supply dates or supplies within 60 days before or after the NSAID supply. Disregard a proton pump inhibitor course known to have ended before the NSAID started or begun after it finished. Suspect a finding for an NSAID course without cover. If an NSAID was supplied as needed and actual use is unclear, or unclear directions leave cover uncertain, report only a possible finding. Ask when the systemic NSAID was taken and whether a proton pump inhibitor covered those days. If the NSAID was never taken, make no finding for that supply. Make no finding for a covered course. Exclude topical NSAIDs.
cannot_be_seen: Whether the person bought a proton pump inhibitor or antacid without a prescription, and whether the NSAID was really taken. Also the person's own risk of stomach bleeding, such as a past ulcer that was never recorded, and medicines supplied by a hospital or another pharmacy.
ask_the_gp: Whether a proton pump inhibitor should be given while the NSAID continues, or whether the NSAID is still needed.
